strengths: The paper provides a systematic and unified comparison of a broad set of Direct Alignment Algorithms (DPO, IPO, SimPO, ORPO, ASFT, APO-Zero, NCA, Cal-DPO) under a common two-stage framework and a shared hyperparameter space, which is useful for the community trying to orient between many similar objectives.

The theoretical reformulations are clean and informative: Appendix B shows that ASFT's alignment loss is exactly the sum of two BCE terms (likelihood + unlikelihood), and Appendix C shows that ORPO is upper-bounded by ASFT, giving a principled reason why ORPO tends to outperform ASFT. These results are useful for interpreting odds-based losses.

The empirical study is comprehensive: two model scales (Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B), two task families (TL;DR summarization, UltraFeedback), three evaluation protocols (AlpacaEval 2 LC/WR, ArenaHard, GPT-4 side-by-side), and Pareto fronts over β–KL.

Two actionable empirical findings emerge: (i) explicitly separating SFT from the alignment loss improves ORPO/ASFT to DPO-comparable levels, and (ii) most methods saturate at only 5–10% of SFT data, which is practically valuable and consistent with prior data-efficiency work.

Reproducibility is good: the appendix reports full hyperparameter grids, β ranges per method, learning-rate sweeps, generation settings, datasets sizes, and the exact GPT-4 evaluation prompt. Hardware and compute budget (602 GPU-days) are stated.

The paper is honest about limitations (off-policy, SFT-based, GPT-based evaluation, instruction-following data only) and does not overclaim novelty of the β parameter, framing unification as a means for fair comparison.

The attempt to explain the pairwise-vs-pointwise gap via prompt-specific bias is a genuinely interesting angle, and using ICC1 (toy experiment and real data) is a reasonable attempt to operationalize that hypothesis.
weaknesses: The central explanatory claim of Section 6 — that the pairwise advantage stems from avoiding prompt-specific-bias 'unlearning' — is only weakly supported. The controlled toy experiment (Appendix E) deliberately discards the scalar-score distinction (r_ref vs r_odds) and operates on scalar prompts/responses with an MLP, so it cannot validate the mechanism in the actual DAA setting the paper is about.

Hyperparameters (λ, β, learning rate) are grid-searched aggressively per method and per β. Because several 'improvements' (e.g., ORPO vs ASFT, pairwise vs pointwise) sit within overlapping confidence intervals in Table 2 and Figure 4, the strength of the reported separations is not fully convincing; some claims of 'significant' gains rely on comparing single best runs rather than seed-level variance.

The headline conclusion that pairwise objectives outperform pointwise ones is largely consistent with long-standing learning-to-rank literature (Liu et al., 2009; Burges et al., 2005) that the paper itself cites, and the empirical separation is only clearly observed at one scale (Llama 3.1 8B UF); on Llama 3.2 3B, the authors acknowledge no clear separation, which weakens the generality of the claim.

Originality is modest. Recasting ORPO/ASFT as two-stage with an explicit SFT and introducing a β scaling on the odds ratio is a relatively direct extension; the main novel contribution is the negative/unifying result that most DAA design differences disappear after unification, which is useful but not a new method or theory.

No seed-level variance is reported for downstream benchmark numbers; the reported CIs are AlpacaEval/ArenaHard evaluation CIs, which capture judge/sampling noise but not training-seed variability. This makes it hard to assess whether the observed differences are reproducible across runs.

The ∇θ derivation in Appendix D is helpful, but the paper does not empirically test the prediction that the odds-ratio score contributes no KL≈0 anchor (Figure 3 right); the claim that β 'implicitly limits update magnitude' is asserted rather than demonstrated in the main text.

Several presentation issues: inconsistent typo-level errors ('performence', 'reserach', 'Stiannon et al.'), a duplicated author slot in the references, and a figure (Figure 3 / Pareto caption mismatch where 'Section 5.3' is referenced under Table 3's caption) that make the manuscript look less than fully polished.

strengths: Provides a systematic, unified empirical comparison of a broad set of DAAs (DPO, IPO, SimPO, ORPO, ASFT, NCA, Cal-DPO, APO-Zero) under a common two-stage, β-parameterized framework, which materially enables fairer head-to-head comparisons than the fragmented individual method papers.

The theoretical decomposition of ASFT into likelihood/unlikelihood (BCE) terms (App. B) and the algebraic relationship L_ORPO = L_ASFT + λ log(π(yw)(1-π(yl)) + π(yl)(1-π(yw))) (App. C) are correct and useful for understanding how odds-based objectives relate to one another.

The mechanistic hypothesis in Section 6 — that pointwise objectives drive prompt-specific baseline scores (marginalized E_y[r(x,y)]) toward collapse/unlearning while pairwise objectives preserve them — is genuinely novel and is probed with both a controlled toy MLP experiment (ICC_1, App. E) and ICC_1 measurements on real data (App. G).
The SFT data-volume ablation (Section 5.4) showing that most DAAs saturate at ~5–10% of UltraChat is a practically useful and clearly presented result.

At the 8B scale (Table 2), the pairwise-vs-pointwise gap (~27–28 vs ~21–23 LC) is substantial and aligns with the stated thesis, and the authors report confidence intervals rather than only point estimates.
weaknesses: The central claim that ranking type (pairwise vs pointwise) is the primary determinant is only clearly supported at 8B; in the 3B UF setup the differences are explicitly within overlapping confidence intervals, so the generality of the headline conclusion is not established and rests on a post-hoc difficulty/capacity argument.

The theoretical argument that 'minimizing L_ASFT automatically minimizes L_ORPO' (Section 3.1) is logically loose: an upper bound being minimized does not in general minimize a distinct lower-bound objective, and the corollary L_ORPO_Align ≤ L_ASFT_Align is a weak justification for ASFT's empirically lower performance. This weakens a load-bearing part of the narrative.

The mechanism story (bias removal vs capacity) is validated primarily on a highly simplified 2D scalar toy MLP; extrapolating this to real LLM alignment is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the real-data ICC_1 results (Fig. 7) are admittedly 'mixed' across setups.

The β-parameter gains for ORPO/ASFT (+13.45/+8.27 AlpacaEval) are essentially the result of giving these methods a DPO-like tuning knob and grid-searching it; framing this as a methodological advance that 'matches established methods' is somewhat overstated, since a well-tuned DPO/IPO is still competitive or better in several cells (e.g., IPO 28.18 LC).

Evaluation is confined to one SFT corpus (UltraChat), one preference set (UltraFeedback), one summarization task (TL;DR), and two model sizes, all off-policy; no on-policy/RLHF (PPO) baseline is included (acknowledged in Limitations), limiting the reach of the conclusions.

Reproducibility is a concern given the reported ~602 GPU-days of training and wide hyperparameter grids (β values, learning rates), which make independent replication and verification of the peak numbers difficult.

Presentation issues: typos ('performence', 'Stiannon'), inconsistent cross-references (Table 1 caption points to Section 5.3 while the table is discussed in 5.1), and the 'blur' framing sits in tension with the strong assertion that ranking type is 'the primary determinant,' making the paper's takeaway messages feel inconsistent.

strengths: Provides a broad, systematic empirical comparison of eight DAA methods under a unified two-stage SFT-then-alignment setup, with multiple models, datasets, and benchmarks; this is a useful reference for the community.

Derives clean relationships for ORPO and ASFT, showing ASFT's alignment term decomposes into independent BCE/likelihood and unlikelihood terms and ORPO relates to ASFT via a bounded correction; this clarifies previously implicit connections.
Demonstrates practical gains from making SFT and β explicit for ORPO/ASFT (+13.45 and +8.27 AlpacaEval 2 LC in the 8B setting) and shows that 5–10% SFT data suffices for near-peak alignment quality.
The finding that pairwise vs. pointwise ranking is a stronger axis than the scalar score (r_ref vs r_odds) is interesting and well motivated, with Pareto-front and toy-experiment evidence.
Reproducibility details are relatively thorough (datasets, hyperparameter grids, compute, generation settings, evaluation prompt), and limitations are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that ranking type is the primary determinant is not fully isolated: pairwise and pointwise objectives also differ in reference-policy dependence, scalar-score choice, and optimization behavior, and the 3B results show overlapping confidence intervals/no clear separation. Statistical significance tests are largely absent.

The prompt-bias/unlearning mechanism is speculative and only partially supported. The toy experiment is simplified, and the real-data ICC1 results are mixed across settings; the link between ICC1 and alignment performance is not conclusively established.

Introducing β to ORPO/ASFT may partly conflate temperature/step-size effects with method quality; gains from extra tuning could reflect a more favorable hyperparameter search rather than a fundamental two-stage or β-specific advantage.

The claim that the SFT term is redundant because it is encapsulated by the alignment term is not fully reconciled with the empirical finding that an explicit SFT stage and removing the SFT term in two-stage training are both beneficial. The optimization explanation remains incomplete.

Evaluation is limited to Llama 3.1/3.2 models on instruction-following and summarization tasks; no mathematical/reasoning domains or on-policy data are covered, despite the discussion of capacity/task difficulty relying on such regimes.
No code/artifact release is mentioned, and the ~602 GPU-days of training make independent replication difficult; GPT-based evaluation also introduces potential evaluator bias that is not analyzed.

strengths: Systematic and broad empirical study: multiple model families (Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen 2.5 7B/14B), two task types (instruction following and math reasoning), plus a judge-free evaluation on math benchmarks for the main claim.

The unification protocol is genuinely useful for the community: converting ORPO/ASFT to two-stage form and adding a β tempering parameter places previously incomparable methods in a shared hyperparameter space, and the empirical gains from β are substantial (e.g., +43.4 win rate on ASFT for TL;DR).

The identification of ranking objective (pairwise vs. pointwise) as a previously under-explored axis is a valuable reframing that complements existing DAA unification efforts. The empirical pattern replicates across datasets, model scales, and scalar score parameterizations (AlphaPO, f-DPO fKL).

The theoretical analysis in Appendix G formalizes a clear structural distinction (pairwise objectives have G_θ(x)=0, pointwise objectives generically do not), which is a clean and checkable argument, and it is supported by a controlled toy experiment with 1000 seeds and ICC_1 analysis on real data.

Statistical rigor: permutation tests over all C(8,4)=70 group assignments, top-3 hyperparameter robustness, confidence intervals, and length-controlled win rates mitigate common pitfalls of preference-alignment evaluation.
Data-efficiency finding (5-10% SFT data reaching ≥95% of full-data performance across DAAs) is a practically useful and actionable insight.

Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameter grids (lr, β, γ/β, epochs), dataset sizes, generation settings, and clear descriptions of experiments; limitations are honestly stated (offline/static scope, GPT-based judges on instruction-following).
weaknesses: The headline claim that ranking type is the primary determinant of quality is supported most convincingly at 8B and Mistral; at 3B scales the confidence intervals overlap and the authors themselves note no clear separation. This narrows the generality and the strength of the central claim.

The theoretical bias-capacity argument predicts only that pointwise objectives generate a first-order incentive to shift b_θ(x); it does not establish that this incentive is what causes the observed performance gap, nor that pointwise optimization is inherently harmful. The link between G_θ(x)≠0 and reduced alignment quality is a plausibility argument, not a derivation, and the toy experiment's mapping to real DAA training is only suggestive.

The proposed β-tempering for ORPO/ASFT is a straightforward rescaling with known analogs in DPO, and is not itself a novel algorithmic contribution; the paper acknowledges this, but it does mean the significance of the technical novelty rests largely on the comparative analysis.

The bias hypothesis is corroborated by ICC_1 on real data that the authors describe as 'mixed' for some setups (Llama 3.2 UF, TL;DR). This weakens the empirical support for the mechanistic story relative to the empirical comparison itself.

While the paper includes math reasoning as a judge-free check, the main instruction-following conclusions rest heavily on AlpacaEval 2 / ArenaHard / GPT-4 judgments. Sensitivity to judge choice (Kimi K2.5 vs GPT-4o) and prompt template is not extensively discussed.

Method ranking seems in places to be driven by best-of-grid choices; the top-3 robustness check partly addresses this, but some individual comparisons (e.g., ORPO vs DPO at 8B: 28.25 vs 26.82) are within a plausible noise band even after LC correction.

The scope is explicitly limited to offline, static binary preference data. This is a valid scoping decision, but it means the conclusions should not be broadly extrapolated to online/iterative alignment, which is the currently dominant practical regime.

Figures in the main body occasionally rely on best-β selection per method, which can favor methods with wider/less stable β sensitivity; the Pareto-front discussion mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and relevant question: which design choices among direct alignment algorithms actually drive downstream alignment quality, and it does so with a broad empirical sweep across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models and both instruction-following and math benchmarks.

The unification of ORPO/ASFT into a two-stage pipeline and the addition of a β scaling factor provide a useful empirical normalization, and the extensive hyperparameter sweeps in the appendix improve transparency.

The negative/unifying result that many DAA differences shrink after tuning is potentially useful, as is the SFT data-efficiency ablation showing most gains are reached with a fraction of the SFT data.
The limitations section acknowledges the offline/static-preference scope and the reliance on GPT-based evaluation, and the training compute and hyperparameter details aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim—that the pairwise-vs-pointwise ranking objective, rather than the scalar-score family, is the primary determinant of DAA quality—is not cleanly established. The compared methods differ in reference policy, probability normalization, loss shape, β/learning-rate scaling, and tuning difficulty, so the observed gaps cannot be attributed to ranking type alone.

The proposed β for ORPO/ASFT is essentially an additional scale parameter already implicit in λ and the learning rate; the large improvements over β=1 may reflect a poorly tuned baseline and a hyperparameter reparameterization rather than a substantive property of odds-ratio DAAs. The paper does not control for effective update magnitude.

The empirical evidence is mixed and post hoc: there is no clear separation at Llama 3.2 3B or Qwen 7B math, separation appears mainly at 8B/14B, and the paper explains this via an informal 'intermediate difficulty/capacity' hypothesis without an independent difficulty measure or validation.

The theoretical argument has technical flaws: the claim that minimizing the ASFT upper bound 'automatically minimizes' ORPO does not follow, and the gradient analysis largely shows the trivial invariance of pairwise losses to uniform score shifts. The toy MLP experiment and ICC1 analysis on real data are insufficient to establish the proposed bias-unlearning mechanism in LLMs, and the real-data ICC1 results are admitted to be mixed.

Evaluation and statistical support are weaker than the framing. AlpacaEval and ArenaHard rely on judge models with known biases, confidence intervals often overlap, and the permutation test p=0.014 is the minimum attainable value under a grouping chosen by the authors; no correction for multiple comparisons or alternative grouping is provided.

Presentation and reference quality are concerning: several references have incorrect years/venues, and the cited 'Kimi K2.5' work appears future-dated or fabricated, which undermines confidence in the manuscript's rigor.

The claimed novelty is overstated: pairwise-vs-pointwise ranking has been studied extensively in learning-to-rank and in recent DAA comparisons. The contribution is primarily empirical, but the empirical isolation is not sufficient to support the strong conclusion.

strengths: Provides a unified two-stage protocol that brings ORPO/ASFT into the same hyperparameter space as DPO-style DAAs by making SFT and beta explicit, enabling controlled comparisons that were previously difficult.

Systematically evaluates a broad set of DAAs across multiple model families and scales (Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.2 3B, Mistral 7B, Qwen 2.5 7B/14B) on both instruction-following and verifiable math-reasoning benchmarks.

The main empirical finding - that pairwise vs. pointwise ranking structure is a primary driver while scalar score type is secondary - is supported by extensive hyperparameter sweeps, Pareto/KL analyses, top-3 robustness checks, and additional scalar-score families (AlphaPO, f-DPO).
The paper goes beyond a pure benchmark by offering a mechanistic explanation via prompt-specific bias, supported by a controlled toy experiment and ICC analysis on real data.
Demonstrates practical data efficiency: most alignment gains are achieved with 5-10% of SFT data, which is a useful and actionable finding.
Reproducibility is reasonably strong: datasets, training details, beta/lr grids, generation hyperparameters, and compute are reported in the appendix; limitations are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The paper does not appear to release code, which slightly limits reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters.

The categorization of some losses as strictly pairwise or pointwise may be oversimplified (e.g., Cal-DPO contains both pairwise and calibration terms; NCA/ASFT are treated as pointwise but have interaction with both chosen and rejected outputs).

The central claim that ranking objective dominates is not uniform across all settings: at Qwen 2.5 7B, pairwise and pointwise methods are comparable, and on TL;DR most methods are statistically similar; the finding is thus regime-dependent.
The scalar-score conclusion ('secondary') is convincing in the tested offline SFT-initialized setting but may not transfer to online/iterative preference optimization, as the authors acknowledge.
Main instruction-following evaluations rely on LLM judges (AlpacaEval/ArenaHard) with known biases, even though math benchmarks and MT-Bench provide useful complementary evidence.

The theoretical analysis of prompt bias works in a hypothetical score-space uniform-shift sense and does not fully prove that parameterized models cannot or do not change prompt bias under pairwise losses.
